assumptions: The natural-number index n counts complete outside-inside cycles, corresponding to the paper's t=t0+2n.
The nonnegative width sequence contracts by at least one half per complete cycle, which is the paired form of Lemma 20.
The even-step relative distance is bounded by the exponential tail displayed in the proof of Lemma 21.
The odd-step relative distance is no larger than the preceding even-step relative distance, as supplied by the monotonicity part of Theorem 13.

formal_statement.lean_header: theorem p24_t3_lemma21_linear_convergence (data : P24Lemma21Data) : every defining width tail is summable, the explicit exponential tail majorizes both cycle distances, is nonnegative, contracts by one half each cycle, and tends to zero
formal_statement.plain_language: The exponential infinite-tail sequence constructed in Lemma 21 is well-defined, bounds both relative distances in every outside-inside cycle, decreases by at least a factor of one half per cycle, and converges to zero.

informal_proof: Compare every shifted width with the geometric sequence of ratio one half to prove summability. Split the first term from each tail and bound the remaining tail by the first width. Exponentiation turns this tail comparison into a square bound; factor x squared minus one to obtain the one-half contraction. Iterate that contraction and squeeze against a geometric sequence to prove convergence to zero.
informal_statement: Lemma 21, reindexed by complete outside-inside cycles: its explicit exponential tail majorizes the two successive relative distances and contracts by a factor of at least one half; hence the majorant tends to zero.

tier_rationale: The proof requires a geometric domination induction, summability and reindexing of infinite real tails, a nonlinear exponential square argument, and a final convergence proof. This is substantial T2-or-harder work. NumStability has no corresponding alternating-scaling or infinite-tail-majorant result, so L receives no material advantage over N.
